sceneHappening: A young man falls from a window in Troas, and Paul's farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus
summary: After the uproar ceases, Paul sends for the disciples, takes his leave, and goes to Macedonia. When he has gone through those parts and encouraged them with many words, he comes into Greece and spends three months there. When the Jews make a plot against him as he is about to set sail for Syria, he decides to return through Macedonia. He is accompanied by Sopater of Beroea, Aristarchus and Secundus of Thessalonica, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia. These go ahead and wait for us at Troas. We sail away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and come to them at Troas in five days, where we stay seven days. On the first day of the week, when the disciples are gathered together to break bread, Paul talks with them, intending to depart the next day, and continues his speech until midnight. There are many lamps in the upper chamber where they are gathered. A certain young man named Eutychus sits in the window, weighed down with deep sleep, and as Paul talks still longer, he sinks down with sleep and falls from the third story, and is taken up dead. Paul goes down, falls on him, and embraces him: "Don't be troubled, for his life is in him." When he has gone up, broken the bread, eaten, and talked with them a long while, even until break of day, he departs. They bring the young man in alive, and are greatly comforted. We go ahead to the ship, sail to Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, and so on to Mitylene, Chios, Samos, and Miletus, for Paul has decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he won't have to spend time in Asia; he is hurrying to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. From Miletus he sends to Ephesus and calls to himself the elders of the assembly. He says, "You yourselves know, from the first day that I set foot in Asia, how I was with you all the time, serving the Lord with all humility, with many tears, and with trials which happened to me by the plots of the Jews; how I didn't shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ. Now, behold, I go bound by the Spirit to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions wait for me. But these things don't count; nor do I hold my life dear to myself, so that I may finish my race with joy, and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the Good News of the grace of God. Now, behold, I know that you all, among whom I went about preaching the Kingdom of God, will see my face no more." "Therefore I testify to you this day that I am clean from the blood of all men, for I didn't shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed therefore to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood. For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn't cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears." "Now, brothers, I entrust you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one's silver, or gold, or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities, and to those who were with me. In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'" When he has spoken these things, he kneels down and prays with them all. They all weep severely, fall on Paul's neck and kiss him, sorrowing most of all because of the word which he had spoken, that they should see his face no more. They bring him on his way to the ship.
whySettingMatters: This chapter has the third "we" section (from Philippi on), which implies the narrator rejoined Paul in Philippi. The collection for the church in Jerusalem, mentioned in Paul's letters (Romans 15:25-27, 1 Corinthians 16:1-4), explains why so many delegates from the churches go with him; Luke does not mention it here. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast. The meeting "on the first day of the week" for the breaking of bread is the earliest clear picture of Sunday worship, and the long talking, the many lamps, and Eutychus (whose name means "fortunate") falling from a third-story window are told with humor; the language says he was "taken up dead," and Paul's words, "his life is in him," are read as a raising. Miletus is about thirty miles south of Ephesus. Paul's address to the Ephesian elders is the only speech in Acts to believers, and it looks back at his ministry and ahead to his suffering. The elders are called "overseers" (episkopoi) and told to "shepherd" the flock, which shows that elder, overseer, and shepherd describe the same role. The "wolves" prefigure the false teaching described in 1 Timothy. "It is more blessed to give than to receive" is attributed to Jesus but is not in the Gospels; it may come from oral tradition. Paul's hard labor shows he refused to take pay from them.

questions: Eutychus falls asleep and falls. What do you do with a story that is both serious and a little funny?
Paul calls himself "clean from the blood of all men." What does he think his responsibility was?
The elders are told to watch for wolves from outside and from among themselves. How does that shape what a leader does?
"It is more blessed to give than to receive." How does Paul's own life illustrate that?
